title: Fairfield Porter’s Lush, Lonely Vision of the World
excerpt: Zachary Fine reviews “Fairfield Porter: What Everyone Knows” at the Art Students League in New York City.
content_html:
The poet John Ashbery, in 1983, said that Fairfield Porter was “perhaps the major American artist of the century.” It’s not praise you can take at face value—Ashbery and Porter were good friends—but it’s a tempting thought. How might a painter of limited technical skill, who mostly depicted coastal landscapes and living rooms in the nineteen-fifties and sixties, be considered a major American artist? “Perhaps” is the key word in Ashbery’s phrase, a little escape hatch that admits how improbable the judgment is while conveying the ambivalence felt by those of us who admire Porter and can’t always say why. I think if you saw a lone painting of his in a junk shop, unsigned and unframed, you’d find it perfectly pleasing and mediocre.

The new exhibition at the Art Students League, “Fairfield Porter: What Everyone Knows,” has the ideal selection to show why he’s often better than his individual pieces. Porter studied at the League under Thomas Hart Benton—one of his classmates was a fellow named Jackson Pollock—and the experience of seeing his work here, as students hustle by with their backpacks and the perfume of turpentine wafts through the air, feels organic and just right. The gallery is evenly and fluorescently lit, and all thirty-five or so of Porter’s featured paintings are in a single room, concentrating his palette of lime greens and creamy yellows and oxblood reds into one bright, soul-cleansing burst.

Everything happened for Porter when he was about forty-five. After flopping around for a few decades and getting zero traction as a painter, he was invited, in 1951, on the recommendation of Elaine de Kooning, to be a critic for ARTnews. The following year, on the recommendation of Elaine’s husband, Willem de Kooning, he had a solo show at Tibor de Nagy Gallery. The gallery’s director, John Bernard Myers, gave Porter the show without even looking at his work, and was baffled when Porter showed up with half a dozen still-lifes and landscapes. In the fifties, to paint anything but a full-throttle abstraction was an efficient way to derail your career. But Porter’s art grew on Myers, a not uncommon experience. Let the paintings breathe for a while, let them interact with one another and with your thoughts, and they’ll meld together with salt breeze and summer light.

An unusually late bloomer, Porter did his best work in the last decade of his life, from the mid-sixties to 1975. Until then, he was still processing his influences. Sometimes he’d channel a bit of Edward Hopper, albeit with a looser wrist—see the lonely house in a field in “Landscape” (1956)—or borrow some lumpy shapes from Marsden Hartley, but the main hurdles were two Frenchmen, Pierre Bonnard and Édouard Vuillard. Porter saw their work in an exhibition in Chicago, in 1938, and never let them go. Like his forebears, Porter painted bourgeois interiors with flat areas of color and dancing floral patterns on wallpaper and furniture. The problem is that, in much of his early work, the colors are drab. Sometimes a dark mustard or pale green sinks a painting, but often there’s a dampening effect applied to everything, so that in a piece like “Armchair on Porch” (1955) all optical sensation is dulled to a minimum.

Thankfully, in the sixties, a light flips on. An extreme case is “Oak Tree” (1969), where sunlight crashes through the branches onto the grass and becomes its own radioactive organism. There’s a whole subgenre of these high-contrast works in Porter’s late style, but my favorites are pieces like “Untitled (View Outside Southampton Studio)” (1968) and “Amherst Campus No. 1” (1969), with their cartographic splotches of foliage. It hadn’t occurred to me until seeing “Amherst” at the Parrish Art Museum, a decade ago, that a painter could use color as a chronological instrument. In “Untitled,” a row of yellow-green trees are painted so phosphorescently on top of the other layers that they effectively chirp: Look here first! Only then can your eye move to the brick-red house, the pale sky, the pockets of shadow. The effect is to re-create not the trees but the flow of the painter’s own aesthetic experience.

Porter credited the Impressionists with being the first to use color as a vehicle of subjectivity, and Bonnard and Vuillard with intensifying that subjectivity, painting their private lives with an anything-goes palette. But the colorist who gave Porter an extra edge was Willem de Kooning. In the fifties, when de Kooning started doing his big, slashing abstractions with wide housepainter’s brushes, Porter said they recalled landscapes in which the colors are “intensely themselves, as if each color had been freed to be.” Colors didn’t have to represent reality or make concessions to it; they were packets of immediate sensation. Porter said he found his own feelings in de Kooning’s hues: a patch of blue expressed the delight of a Maine summer; pink was the way he felt on the seacoast; a harmony of warm tones bottled up the sensation of autumn. He once compared de Kooning’s use of paint to the “perfect orgasm.”

Most artists enchanted with de Kooning try to paint like him. But Porter somehow passed through the needle’s eye of abstraction and returned to his own eccentric realism on the other side, churning out images of starched Southampton interiors and Penobscot Bay. There are pieces in the show, like “Islands” (1968) and “View from the Front” (ca. 1969), where you can see Porter using what he called the “dry speed” of de Kooning’s brushwork. In “Islands,” there’s an excellent sky-blue brushstroke that horizontally slices the green bush (or is it a tree?) near the middle of the painting. That single stroke implies either that the water is behind the shrub, visible only in patches through the leaves, or that we’re looking at a retinal afterimage of the water over the shrub, as the painter swivels his head between the landscape and the canvas. There’s also a little geyser on the far left, shooting upward like the vertical blast of paint through de Kooning’s “Merritt Parkway” (1959). Ocean spray doesn’t look that way, but it feels like it.

Good painters rarely make good critics, but Porter was both. His writing was rhetorically pungent and had a rare jargon-free poetry. His most exotic idea was to delete fiftyish years of art history and suggest that Impressionism—not Cubism or Surrealism or any other stylistic eruption—was the real forerunner of Abstract Expressionism. A painting obtained reality just by transmitting the artist’s own “kinetic and visual sense of the world,” Porter wrote. This was an indirect jab at his favorite nemesis, the critic Clement Greenberg, whose lockjawed aesthetic program presented Ab Ex as an expression of History itself, which marched in only one direction: from figuration and depth to abstraction and flatness. Greenberg represented the greatest sin for Porter—letting ideas overrule experience. Ideas made painters and critics impervious to seeing what was in front of them. Porter’s mission was to make people see again.

For whatever reason, Porter couldn’t see people. His portraits are almost comically bad. The painter Larry Rivers described Porter’s portrait of him as “flat and rather empty,” and that applies to pretty much all of them. (For the comic element, consider his painting of Frank O’Hara, who looks a bit like a salami sliding off a couch.) None of Porter’s talent for shadow, light, and air transfers to bodies and faces. With “The Screen Porch” (1964), a large group portrait that desperately wants to be a masterpiece—it has a number of auteur touches, like a cannister of turpentine in the bottom left which signals “the painter was here”—Porter’s family had the right idea, nicknaming it “The Four Ugly People.” The only portrait in the exhibition with a spark is “Jimmy and John” (1957-58), of the poets James Schuyler and John Ashbery. Their friendship isn’t visible, nor are their personalities, but the way their bodies are angled away from each other evokes two ships crossing in open water. Just that simple arrangement makes the distance between them ache.

Although Porter was kept at arm’s length by most of the Abstract Expressionists, he was embraced by the New York School poets—in particular Ashbery, Schuyler, O’Hara, and Kenneth Koch—who, almost twenty years his junior, adopted him as a mixed-use transferential figure. To Schuyler, whose relationship with him was the most complicated, Porter was a father figure, a lover, a caretaker, a friend, and a rather sullen, insecure man who needed cheering up. The phrase “conflict of interest” doesn’t begin to describe the kinds of transactions that took place, as Schuyler boosted Porter’s paintings in exhibition reviews even while he was staying at the painter’s house in Southampton, with Porter’s wife and children, and living on his dime. Porter’s family wealth came from land around the present-day Chicago Loop, and he spent much of his life supported by a trust. From the late forties on, he shuttled between his family’s private island in Maine, Great Spruce Head, and the chilly, Federal-style house in Southampton, along with frequent stays in New York City. His wealth worked like a “cotton padding” between him and the world, a friend once said.

Porter didn’t disagree. By some accounts, he was an odd guy. Pleasantries eluded him. If he wasn’t silent altogether, he might start talking intensely about one subject or another, and then fall silent again. He had a kind of estranged personality, with thick walls separating him from different parts of himself and from other people, and it can be felt in not just the portraits but the landscapes. Whether it’s “Looking Through the House” (1961), a darkened interior with a window facing a bay, or “A Day Indoors” (1962), with three sitters in the house on Great Spruce Head, siloed in their own worlds, everything and everyone feels just slightly out of reach. There is a landscape you want to see, as if for the first time, or a person you want to speak to, and for some reason can’t. So much of the feeling in Porter’s work comes from this stuckness. It’s one of the most difficult emotions to convey in art—the emotion that hasn’t yet found its expression—but Porter mastered it. ♦

sentences.zh: 有时他会借鉴爱德华·霍珀的一点，尽管手腕比较宽松——比如《风景》（1956）中田野里孤独的房子——或者从马斯登·哈特利那里借用一些凹凸不平的形状，但主要的障碍是两个法国人，皮埃尔·博纳尔和爱德华·维亚尔。

sentences.en: Porter saw their work in an exhibition in Chicago, in 1938, and never let them go.
sentences.zh: 1938 年，波特在芝加哥的一次展览中看到了他们的作品，从此再也没有放过他们。

sentences.en: Like his forebears, Porter painted bourgeois interiors with flat areas of color and dancing floral patterns on wallpaper and furniture.
sentences.zh: 和他的祖先一样，波特在壁纸和家具上用平坦的颜色和舞动的花卉图案绘制了资产阶级室内装饰。

sentences.en: The problem is that, in much of his early work, the colors are drab.
sentences.zh: 问题是，在他早期的大部分作品中，颜色都是单调的。

sentences.en: Sometimes a dark mustard or pale green sinks a painting, but often there’s a dampening effect applied to everything, so that in a piece like “Armchair on Porch” (1955) all optical sensation is dulled to a minimum.
sentences.zh: 有时，深芥末色或淡绿色会使一幅画下沉，但通常会对所有事物施加阻尼效果，因此在像“门廊上的扶手椅”（1955）这样的作品中，所有视觉感觉都被减弱到最低限度。

blocks.html_en: Thankfully, in the sixties, a light flips on. An extreme case is “Oak Tree” (1969), where sunlight crashes through the branches onto the grass and becomes its own radioactive organism. There’s a whole subgenre of these high-contrast works in Porter’s late style, but my favorites are pieces like “Untitled (View Outside Southampton Studio)” (1968) and “Amherst Campus No. 1” (1969), with their cartographic splotches of foliage. It hadn’t occurred to me until seeing “Amherst” at the Parrish Art Museum, a decade ago, that a painter could use color as a chronological instrument. In “Untitled,” a row of yellow-green trees are painted so phosphorescently on top of the other layers that they effectively chirp: Look here first! Only then can your eye move to the brick-red house, the pale sky, the pockets of shadow. The effect is to re-create not the trees but the flow of the painter’s own aesthetic experience.

sentences.en: Thankfully, in the sixties, a light flips on.
sentences.zh: 值得庆幸的是，在六十年代，一盏灯亮了起来。

sentences.en: An extreme case is “Oak Tree” (1969), where sunlight crashes through the branches onto the grass and becomes its own radioactive organism.
sentences.zh: 一个极端的例子是《橡树》（1969），阳光透过树枝照射到草地上，变成了它自己的放射性有机体。

sentences.en: There’s a whole subgenre of these high-contrast works in Porter’s late style, but my favorites are pieces like “Untitled (View Outside Southampton Studio)” (1968) and “Amherst Campus No. 1” (1969), with their cartographic splotches of foliage.
sentences.zh: 波特晚期风格的这些高对比度作品有一个完整的子流派，但我最喜欢的是像“无题（南安普顿工作室外的景色）”（1968）和“阿默斯特校园一号”（1969）这样的作品，上面有树叶的地图斑点。

sentences.en: It hadn’t occurred to me until seeing “Amherst” at the Parrish Art Museum, a decade ago, that a painter could use color as a chronological instrument.
sentences.zh: 直到十年前在帕里什艺术博物馆看到“阿默斯特”时，我才想到画家可以使用颜色作为时间顺序的工具。

sentences.en: In “Untitled,” a row of yellow-green trees are painted so phosphorescently on top of the other layers that they effectively chirp: Look here first!
sentences.zh: 在《无题》中，一排黄绿色的树在其他图层的顶部被涂上了磷光，以至于它们有效地鸣叫：先看这里！

sentences.en: Only then can your eye move to the brick-red house, the pale sky, the pockets of shadow.
sentences.zh: 只有这样，你的目光才能转移到砖红色的房子、苍白的天空、阴影的地方。

sentences.en: The effect is to re-create not the trees but the flow of the painter’s own aesthetic experience.
sentences.zh: 其效果不是重新创造树木，而是画家自身审美体验的流动。

blocks.html_en: Porter credited the Impressionists with being the first to use color as a vehicle of subjectivity, and Bonnard and Vuillard with intensifying that subjectivity, painting their private lives with an anything-goes palette. But the colorist who gave Porter an extra edge was Willem de Kooning. In the fifties, when de Kooning started doing his big, slashing abstractions with wide housepainter’s brushes, Porter said they recalled landscapes in which the colors are “intensely themselves, as if each color had been freed to be.” Colors didn’t have to represent reality or make concessions to it; they were packets of immediate sensation. Porter said he found his own feelings in de Kooning’s hues: a patch of blue expressed the delight of a Maine summer; pink was the way he felt on the seacoast; a harmony of warm tones bottled up the sensation of autumn. He once compared de Kooning’s use of paint to the “perfect orgasm.”

sentences.en: Porter credited the Impressionists with being the first to use color as a vehicle of subjectivity, and Bonnard and Vuillard with intensifying that subjectivity, painting their private lives with an anything-goes palette.
sentences.zh: 波特认为印象派画家是第一个使用色彩作为主观性载体的人，而博纳尔和维亚尔则强化了这种主观性，用随心所欲的调色板描绘他们的私人生活。

sentences.en: But the colorist who gave Porter an extra edge was Willem de Kooning.
sentences.zh: 但给波特带来额外优势的调色师是威廉·德·库宁。

sentences.en: In the fifties, when de Kooning started doing his big, slashing abstractions with wide housepainter’s brushes, Porter said they recalled landscapes in which the colors are “intensely themselves, as if each color had been freed to be.”
sentences.zh: 五十年代，当德库宁开始用宽阔的房屋画家画笔创作他的大型、锐利的抽象画时，波特说，他们回忆起风景中的颜色“强烈地表达自己，就好像每种颜色都被释放了一样。”

sentences.en: Colors didn’t have to represent reality or make concessions to it; they were packets of immediate sensation.
sentences.zh: 颜色不必代表现实或向现实做出让步；它们是即时感觉的包。

sentences.en: Porter said he found his own feelings in de Kooning’s hues: a patch of blue expressed the delight of a Maine summer; pink was the way he felt on the seacoast; a harmony of warm tones bottled up the sensation of autumn.
sentences.zh: 波特说，他在德库宁的色调中找到了自己的感觉：一片蓝色表达了缅因州夏天的愉悦；粉红色是他在海岸上的感觉；温暖的色调和谐地包裹着秋天的感觉。

sentences.en: He once compared de Kooning’s use of paint to the “perfect orgasm.”
sentences.zh: 他曾将德库宁对颜料的使用比作“完美的高潮”。

blocks.html_en: Most artists enchanted with de Kooning try to paint like him. But Porter somehow passed through the needle’s eye of abstraction and returned to his own eccentric realism on the other side, churning out images of starched Southampton interiors and Penobscot Bay. There are pieces in the show, like “Islands” (1968) and “View from the Front” (ca. 1969), where you can see Porter using what he called the “dry speed” of de Kooning’s brushwork. In “Islands,” there’s an excellent sky-blue brushstroke that horizontally slices the green bush (or is it a tree?) near the middle of the painting. That single stroke implies either that the water is behind the shrub, visible only in patches through the leaves, or that we’re looking at a retinal afterimage of the water over the shrub, as the painter swivels his head between the landscape and the canvas. There’s also a little geyser on the far left, shooting upward like the vertical blast of paint through de Kooning’s “Merritt Parkway” (1959). Ocean spray doesn’t look that way, but it feels like it.

sentences.en: Most artists enchanted with de Kooning try to paint like him.
sentences.zh: 大多数对德库宁着迷的艺术家都尝试像他一样绘画。

sentences.en: But Porter somehow passed through the needle’s eye of abstraction and returned to his own eccentric realism on the other side, churning out images of starched Southampton interiors and Penobscot Bay.
sentences.zh: 但波特不知怎么地穿过了抽象的针眼，回到了他自己古怪的现实主义另一边，大量制作了南安普敦内饰和佩诺布斯科特湾的图像。

sentences.en: There are pieces in the show, like “Islands” (1968) and “View from the Front” (ca. 1969), where you can see Porter using what he called the “dry speed” of de Kooning’s brushwork.
sentences.zh: 展览中的一些作品，如《岛屿》（Islands）（1968年）和《前视图》（View from the Front）（约1969年），你可以看到波特使用他所谓的德库宁笔触的“干速度”。

sentences.en: In “Islands,” there’s an excellent sky-blue brushstroke that horizontally slices the green bush (or is it a tree?)
sentences.zh: 在《岛屿》中，有一个出色的天蓝色笔触，水平地切开了绿色的灌木（或者是一棵树？）

sentences.en: near the middle of the painting.
sentences.zh: 靠近画的中间。

sentences.en: That single stroke implies either that the water is behind the shrub, visible only in patches through the leaves, or that we’re looking at a retinal afterimage of the water over the shrub, as the painter swivels his head between the landscape and the canvas.
sentences.zh: 这一笔画要么暗示着水在灌木后面，只能透过树叶看到一些斑点，要么意味着当画家在风景和画布之间旋转头部时，我们正在看到灌木上水的视网膜残像。

sentences.en: There’s also a little geyser on the far left, shooting upward like the vertical blast of paint through de Kooning’s “Merritt Parkway” (1959).
sentences.zh: 最左边还有一个小间歇泉，向上喷射，就像德库宁的《梅里特公园路》（Merritt Parkway，1959）中垂直喷射的油漆一样。

sentences.en: Ocean spray doesn’t look that way, but it feels like it.
sentences.zh: 海洋浪花看起来不像那样，但感觉起来却很像。

blocks.html_en: Good painters rarely make good critics, but Porter was both. His writing was rhetorically pungent and had a rare jargon-free poetry. His most exotic idea was to delete fiftyish years of art history and suggest that Impressionism—not Cubism or Surrealism or any other stylistic eruption—was the real forerunner of Abstract Expressionism. A painting obtained reality just by transmitting the artist’s own “kinetic and visual sense of the world,” Porter wrote. This was an indirect jab at his favorite nemesis, the critic Clement Greenberg, whose lockjawed aesthetic program presented Ab Ex as an expression of History itself, which marched in only one direction: from figuration and depth to abstraction and flatness. Greenberg represented the greatest sin for Porter—letting ideas overrule experience. Ideas made painters and critics impervious to seeing what was in front of them. Porter’s mission was to make people see again.

sentences.en: Good painters rarely make good critics, but Porter was both.
sentences.zh: 优秀的画家很少能成为优秀的批评家，但波特两者兼而有之。

sentences.en: His writing was rhetorically pungent and had a rare jargon-free poetry.
sentences.zh: 他的作品修辞辛辣，诗歌中少有的没有行话。

sentences.en: His most exotic idea was to delete fiftyish years of art history and suggest that Impressionism—not Cubism or Surrealism or any other stylistic eruption—was the real forerunner of Abstract Expressionism.
sentences.zh: 他最奇特的想法是删除五十年的艺术史，并表明印象派——而不是立体主义、超现实主义或任何其他风格爆发——才是抽象表现主义的真正先驱。

sentences.en: A painting obtained reality just by transmitting the artist’s own “kinetic and visual sense of the world,” Porter wrote.
sentences.zh: 波特写道，一幅画仅仅通过传递艺术家自己的“对世界的动感和视觉感”就获得了现实。

sentences.en: This was an indirect jab at his favorite nemesis, the critic Clement Greenberg, whose lockjawed aesthetic program presented Ab Ex as an expression of History itself, which marched in only one direction: from figuration and depth to abstraction and flatness.
sentences.zh: 这是对他最喜欢的对手、批评家克莱门特·格林伯格的间接攻击，他那张牙关紧闭的美学纲领将抽象表现主义呈现为历史本身的一种表达，而它只朝着一个方向前进：从具象和深度到抽象和平面。

sentences.en: Greenberg represented the greatest sin for Porter—letting ideas overrule experience.
sentences.zh: 格林伯格代表了波特最大的罪过——让想法凌驾于经验之上。

sentences.en: Ideas made painters and critics impervious to seeing what was in front of them.
sentences.zh: 想法使画家和评论家无法看到眼前的事物。

sentences.en: Porter’s mission was to make people see again.
sentences.zh: 波特的使命是让人们重见光明。

blocks.html_en: For whatever reason, Porter couldn’t see people. His portraits are almost comically bad. The painter Larry Rivers described Porter’s portrait of him as “flat and rather empty,” and that applies to pretty much all of them. (For the comic element, consider his painting of Frank O’Hara, who looks a bit like a salami sliding off a couch.) None of Porter’s talent for shadow, light, and air transfers to bodies and faces. With “The Screen Porch” (1964), a large group portrait that desperately wants to be a masterpiece—it has a number of auteur touches, like a cannister of turpentine in the bottom left which signals “the painter was here”—Porter’s family had the right idea, nicknaming it “The Four Ugly People.” The only portrait in the exhibition with a spark is “Jimmy and John” (1957-58), of the poets James Schuyler and John Ashbery. Their friendship isn’t visible, nor are their personalities, but the way their bodies are angled away from each other evokes two ships crossing in open water. Just that simple arrangement makes the distance between them ache.

sentences.en: For whatever reason, Porter couldn’t see people.
sentences.zh: 不管出于什么原因，波特看不见人。

sentences.en: His portraits are almost comically bad.
sentences.zh: 他的肖像画糟糕得几乎可笑。

sentences.en: The painter Larry Rivers described Porter’s portrait of him as “flat and rather empty,” and that applies to pretty much all of them.

sentences.en: With “The Screen Porch” (1964), a large group portrait that desperately wants to be a masterpiece—it has a number of auteur touches, like a cannister of turpentine in the bottom left which signals “the painter was here”—Porter’s family had the right idea, nicknaming it “The Four Ugly People.”

blocks.html_en: Although Porter was kept at arm’s length by most of the Abstract Expressionists, he was embraced by the New York School poets—in particular Ashbery, Schuyler, O’Hara, and Kenneth Koch—who, almost twenty years his junior, adopted him as a mixed-use transferential figure. To Schuyler, whose relationship with him was the most complicated, Porter was a father figure, a lover, a caretaker, a friend, and a rather sullen, insecure man who needed cheering up. The phrase “conflict of interest” doesn’t begin to describe the kinds of transactions that took place, as Schuyler boosted Porter’s paintings in exhibition reviews even while he was staying at the painter’s house in Southampton, with Porter’s wife and children, and living on his dime. Porter’s family wealth came from land around the present-day Chicago Loop, and he spent much of his life supported by a trust. From the late forties on, he shuttled between his family’s private island in Maine, Great Spruce Head, and the chilly, Federal-style house in Southampton, along with frequent stays in New York City. His wealth worked like a “cotton padding” between him and the world, a friend once said.

sentences.en: Although Porter was kept at arm’s length by most of the Abstract Expressionists, he was embraced by the New York School poets—in particular Ashbery, Schuyler, O’Hara, and Kenneth Koch—who, almost twenty years his junior, adopted him as a mixed-use transferential figure.

blocks.html_en: Porter didn’t disagree. By some accounts, he was an odd guy. Pleasantries eluded him. If he wasn’t silent altogether, he might start talking intensely about one subject or another, and then fall silent again. He had a kind of estranged personality, with thick walls separating him from different parts of himself and from other people, and it can be felt in not just the portraits but the landscapes. Whether it’s “Looking Through the House” (1961), a darkened interior with a window facing a bay, or “A Day Indoors” (1962), with three sitters in the house on Great Spruce Head, siloed in their own worlds, everything and everyone feels just slightly out of reach. There is a landscape you want to see, as if for the first time, or a person you want to speak to, and for some reason can’t. So much of the feeling in Porter’s work comes from this stuckness. It’s one of the most difficult emotions to convey in art—the emotion that hasn’t yet found its expression—but Porter mastered it. ♦

sentences.en: Porter didn’t disagree.
sentences.zh: 波特没有反对。

sentences.en: By some accounts, he was an odd guy.

sentences.zh: 他没有感到愉快。

sentences.en: If he wasn’t silent altogether, he might start talking intensely about one subject or another, and then fall silent again.
sentences.zh: 如果他不是完全沉默，他可能会开始激烈地谈论一个或另一个话题，然后又陷入沉默。

sentences.en: He had a kind of estranged personality, with thick walls separating him from different parts of himself and from other people, and it can be felt in not just the portraits but the landscapes.

content_html_zh:
1983 年，诗人约翰·阿什伯里 (John Ashbery) 表示，费尔菲尔德·波特“也许是本世纪最重要的美国艺术家”。 这不是表面上的赞美——阿什伯里和波特是好朋友——但这是一个诱人的想法。 一个技术水平有限、主要描绘十九世纪五六十年代沿海风景和客厅的画家，如何能被视为美国重要艺术家呢？ “也许”是阿什伯里这句话中的关键词，它是一个小小的逃生口，它承认这个判断是多么不可能，同时也传达了我们这些钦佩波特但总是无法说出原因的人所感受到的矛盾心理。 我想，如果你在旧货店里看到他的一幅孤独的画，没有签名，也没有装框，你会发现它非常令人愉悦，而且很平庸。

艺术学生联盟的新展览“费尔菲尔德·波特：每个人都知道的事情”是展示他为什么往往比他的个人作品更好的理想选择。 波特在托马斯·哈特·本顿（Thomas Hart Benton）的联盟学院学习——他的一个同学是杰克逊·波洛克（Jackson Pollock）——在这里看到他的作品，当学生背着背包匆匆走过，松节油的香味在空气中飘荡时，感觉有机而恰到好处。 画廊里的荧光灯照明均匀，波特大约三十五幅特色画作都集中在一个房间里，他的柠檬绿、奶油黄和深红色集中在明亮的、净化灵魂的色彩中。

波特四十五岁时，一切都发生了。 在徘徊了几十年、作为一名画家的影响力为零之后，1951 年，在伊莱恩·德·库宁的推荐下，他被邀请担任 ARTnews 的评论家。 次年，在伊莱恩的丈夫威廉·德·库宁的推荐下，他在蒂博·德·纳吉画廊举办了个展。 画廊总监约翰·伯纳德·迈尔斯 (John Bernard Myers) 甚至没有看波特的作品就给他举办了这场展览，当波特带着六幅静物画和风景画出现时，他感到很困惑。 在五十年代，除了全速抽象之外，画任何东西都是让你的职业生涯脱轨的有效方式。 但波特的艺术是在迈尔斯的影响下成长起来的，这种经历并不罕见。 让画作呼吸一会儿，让它们彼此互动，与你的思想互动，它们就会与咸咸的微风和夏日的阳光融为一体。

波特是个大器晚成的人，他在生命的最后十年（从 60 年代中期到 1975 年）取得了最好的成就。 在那之前，他仍在处理他的影响。 有时他会借鉴爱德华·霍珀的一点，尽管手腕比较宽松——比如《风景》（1956）中田野里孤独的房子——或者从马斯登·哈特利那里借用一些凹凸不平的形状，但主要的障碍是两个法国人，皮埃尔·博纳尔和爱德华·维亚尔。 1938 年，波特在芝加哥的一次展览中看到了他们的作品，从此再也没有放过他们。 和他的祖先一样，波特在壁纸和家具上用平坦的颜色和舞动的花卉图案绘制了资产阶级室内装饰。 问题是，在他早期的大部分作品中，颜色都是单调的。 有时，深芥末色或淡绿色会使一幅画下沉，但通常会对所有事物施加阻尼效果，因此在像“门廊上的扶手椅”（1955）这样的作品中，所有视觉感觉都被减弱到最低限度。

值得庆幸的是，在六十年代，一盏灯亮了起来。 一个极端的例子是《橡树》（1969），阳光透过树枝照射到草地上，变成了它自己的放射性有机体。 波特晚期风格的这些高对比度作品有一个完整的子流派，但我最喜欢的是像“无题（南安普顿工作室外的景色）”（1968）和“阿默斯特校园一号”（1969）这样的作品，上面有树叶的地图斑点。 直到十年前在帕里什艺术博物馆看到“阿默斯特”时，我才想到画家可以使用颜色作为时间顺序的工具。 在《无题》中，一排黄绿色的树在其他图层的顶部被涂上了磷光，以至于它们有效地鸣叫：先看这里！ 只有这样，你的目光才能转移到砖红色的房子、苍白的天空、阴影的地方。 其效果不是重新创造树木，而是画家自身审美体验的流动。

波特认为印象派画家是第一个使用色彩作为主观性载体的人，而博纳尔和维亚尔则强化了这种主观性，用随心所欲的调色板描绘他们的私人生活。 但给波特带来额外优势的调色师是威廉·德·库宁。 五十年代，当德库宁开始用宽阔的房屋画家画笔创作他的大型、锐利的抽象画时，波特说，他们回忆起风景中的颜色“强烈地表达自己，就好像每种颜色都被释放了一样。” 颜色不必代表现实或向现实做出让步；它们是即时感觉的包。 波特说，他在德库宁的色调中找到了自己的感觉：一片蓝色表达了缅因州夏天的愉悦；粉红色是他在海岸上的感觉；温暖的色调和谐地包裹着秋天的感觉。 他曾将德库宁对颜料的使用比作“完美的高潮”。

大多数对德库宁着迷的艺术家都尝试像他一样绘画。 但波特不知怎么地穿过了抽象的针眼，回到了他自己古怪的现实主义另一边，大量制作了南安普敦内饰和佩诺布斯科特湾的图像。 展览中的一些作品，如《岛屿》（Islands）（1968年）和《前视图》（View from the Front）（约1969年），你可以看到波特使用他所谓的德库宁笔触的“干速度”。 在《岛屿》中，有一个出色的天蓝色笔触，水平地切开了绿色的灌木（或者是一棵树？） 靠近画的中间。 这一笔画要么暗示着水在灌木后面，只能透过树叶看到一些斑点，要么意味着当画家在风景和画布之间旋转头部时，我们正在看到灌木上水的视网膜残像。 最左边还有一个小间歇泉，向上喷射，就像德库宁的《梅里特公园路》（Merritt Parkway，1959）中垂直喷射的油漆一样。 海洋浪花看起来不像那样，但感觉起来却很像。

优秀的画家很少能成为优秀的批评家，但波特两者兼而有之。 他的作品修辞辛辣，诗歌中少有的没有行话。 他最奇特的想法是删除五十年的艺术史，并表明印象派——而不是立体主义、超现实主义或任何其他风格爆发——才是抽象表现主义的真正先驱。 波特写道，一幅画仅仅通过传递艺术家自己的“对世界的动感和视觉感”就获得了现实。 这是对他最喜欢的对手、批评家克莱门特·格林伯格的间接攻击，他那张牙关紧闭的美学纲领将抽象表现主义呈现为历史本身的一种表达，而它只朝着一个方向前进：从具象和深度到抽象和平面。 格林伯格代表了波特最大的罪过——让想法凌驾于经验之上。 想法使画家和评论家无法看到眼前的事物。 波特的使命是让人们重见光明。

不管出于什么原因，波特看不见人。 他的肖像画糟糕得几乎可笑。 画家拉里·里弗斯 (Larry Rivers) 将波特的肖像描述为“扁平且相当空虚”，这几乎适用于所有人。 （对于喜剧元素，请考虑他画的弗兰克·奥哈拉（Frank O’Hara），他看起来有点像从沙发上滑下来的萨拉米香肠。） 波特在阴影、光线和空气方面的天赋都没有转移到身体和面孔上。 《屏风门廊》（The Screen Porch，1964）是一幅大型群像，迫切希望成为一部杰作——它有很多作者的风格，比如左下角的一罐松节油，表明“画家在这里”——波特的家人有正确的想法，给它起了个绰号“四个丑陋的人”。 展览中唯一有火花的肖像是诗人詹姆斯·斯凯勒和约翰·阿什伯里的《吉米和约翰》（1957-58）。 他们的友谊不可见，他们的个性也不可见，但他们的身体彼此倾斜的方式让人想起两艘船在开阔的水域中穿越。 就是这样简单的安排，却让他们之间的距离变得疼痛。

尽管波特被大多数抽象表现主义者敬而远之，但他却受到了纽约学派诗人的欢迎，特别是阿什贝里、斯凯勒、奥哈拉和肯尼思·科赫，他们比他小了近二十岁，把他视为一个混合用途的移情人物。 对于与波特的关系最为复杂的斯凯勒来说，波特是一个父亲的角色、一个情人、一个看护者、一个朋友，也是一个阴沉、缺乏安全感、需要振作起来的人。 “利益冲突”一词并不足以描述所发生的交易类型，因为斯凯勒在展览评论中宣传了波特的画作，即使他与波特的妻子和孩子一起住在南安普敦画家的家里，靠自己的钱生活。 波特的家族财富来自现今芝加哥环线周围的土地，他一生的大部分时间都靠信托基金支持。 从四十年代末开始，他穿梭于家族位于缅因州的私人岛屿大云杉角和南安普敦寒冷的联邦风格房屋之间，并经常在纽约市逗留。 一位朋友曾经说过，他的财富就像他和世界之间的“棉垫”一样。

波特没有反对。 从某些方面来看，他是一个奇怪的人。 他没有感到愉快。 如果他不是完全沉默，他可能会开始激烈地谈论一个或另一个话题，然后又陷入沉默。 他有一种疏远的性格，厚重的墙壁将他与自己和其他人的不同部分隔开，这一点不仅可以在肖像画中感受到，在风景画中也能感受到。 无论是《Looking Through the House》（1961），一个黑暗的室内，窗户面向海湾，还是《A Day Indoors》（1962），三个坐在大云杉角房子里的人，被困在自己的世界里，一切和每个人都感觉有点遥不可及。 你想看到一处风景，就像第一次看到一样，或者你想与一个人交谈，但由于某种原因不能。 波特作品中的很多感觉都来自于这种停滞。 这是艺术中最难表达的情感之一——尚未找到表达方式的情感——但波特掌握了它。 ❖
